“Meis mitzvah1!” a trembling voice rang out in the Cracow marketplace.

This time, the voice totally silenced the shoppers and vendors scattered about the cobblestone square. Everyone— from the line in front of the fishmonger to the women clustered around the baker to the children chasing the apples that had rolled away from the fruit stand—turned to find the source of the call. At the edge of the market stood a man, a stranger

occasions, he’d be in the castle of a local poritz5 or prince, signing a business deal or trade agreement. Still other times, he’d be pacing the offices of the community hall, outlining a new plan to improve the kehillah.

But what really set Reb Yosef apart was his character. Never would he turn a beggar away from his door; his knowledge of both Torah and secular wisdom was vast; and he had a way of making everyone he knew feel like they were Yosef’s best friend. Everyone in Cracow—Jew and gentile, rich and poor—would miss Reb Yosef.

was newly married. Sadly, this was not the first loss for Rosa*, Reb Yosef’s young widow. Not too long before, she had been orphaned from her father, Reb Avraham the Goldsmith. Additionally, Rosa and Yosef hadn’t had any children. Now, aside from her mother, Rosa had no one in the world.

Soon after the funeral, Rosa went to do chalitza6 with Reb Yosef’s brother, allowing her to remarry. It was the practice in Cracow for the entire community to gather and watch the ceremony.

After the chalitza was complete, the shamash made the customary announcement: “If there is anyone here who wants to marry this righteous chalutza7, he should step forward! Great brachos are promised for such a marriage.”

No one stepped forward. Rosa returned, alone, to her mother’s home.
